claims.text: The initial catalyst is a near-equiatomic multi-principal-element automotive alloy containing Cu, Ni, Pd, and Pt in nearly equal ratios.
The initial catalyst uses minimal platinum.
A conformal 2–5 nm CeO2 coating will be deposited on the catalyst by sol-gel processing or atomic layer deposition.
Adding the CeO2 overlayer will preserve low platinum-group-metal usage.
The ultrathin CeO2 overlayer will act as an oxygen buffer.
The ultrathin CeO2 overlayer will act as a physical barrier.
The CeO2 overlayer will preserve finely dispersed active sites and retard sintering.
The CeO2 overlayer will retard surface poisoning.
CeO2 oxygen storage and release will enhance low-temperature oxidation reactions.
The CeO2 layer will reduce adsorption of H2O and NO on active sites.
The CeO2 layer will stabilize the catalyst structure during thermal cycling.
Relative to the unmodified catalyst, the coated catalyst will have lower light-off temperatures for CO oxidation.
Relative to the unmodified catalyst, the coated catalyst will have lower light-off temperatures for hydrocarbon oxidation.
Relative to the unmodified catalyst, the coated catalyst will have greater resistance to poisoning by H2O and NO.
Relative to the unmodified catalyst, the coated catalyst will degrade more slowly during extended transient low-temperature operation.
The unmodified catalyst has performance limitations under low-temperature, transient, and poisoning conditions.
The unmodified catalyst undergoes notable degradation during lifetime aging.
The predicted improvements apply below 150 °C, in H2O- and NO-containing transient exhaust, and through approximately 1000 hours of accelerated aging.

contradictions.description: A nearly equal-ratio Cu–Ni–Pd–Pt alloy would contain a large combined Pd/Pt fraction, which is in tension with the statements that platinum use and overall platinum-group-metal usage are low.
